relations.note: Mahākāla is a terrible black, temporal, and death-associated form of Śiva.
Daikokuten is presented as an emanation of Maheśvara.
Vairocana assumes or deploys Mahākāla’s form to restrain murderous demonesses.
Mahākāla governs, subdues, or converts the Mothers and their dangerous appetites.
In Mahākāla form, he stops the spirits killing humans and redirects them to Dharma service.
Mahākāla travels nocturnally with a host consuming human flesh and vital essence.
Bishamonten supplies one face and defensive, treasure-bestowing aspect of the composite deity.
Benzaiten supplies one face and an eloquent, musical, watery fortune aspect.
Homophonic readings of Great Black and Great Country supported their medieval equation.

relations.myth: Miwa god appears in Daikoku form
relations.note: The Miwa deity appears as Daikoku Tenshin, provides wood, and protects Hiei’s foundation.
Daikokuten and Hiei’s Sannō complex became overlapping protectors of Enryakuji.
Daikoku and Ebisu jointly bestow agricultural, maritime, commercial, and household fortune.
When identified with Ōkuninushi, Daikoku becomes father of Ebisu identified as Kotoshironushi.
Through Ōkuninushi, Daikoku secondarily inherits Sukunabikona’s assistance in developing the land.
Through Ōkuninushi, Daikoku inherits Susanoo’s ordeals and eventual authorization of his rule.
Daikoku secondarily inherits Ōkuninushi’s marriage to Suseribime and their escape.

relations.myth: Healing the White Hare of Inaba
relations.note: Through Ōkuninushi, Daikoku secondarily inherits the episode of healing the injured hare.
Through Ōkuninushi, Daikoku inherits the surrender of earthly rule to Amaterasu’s line.
Through Ōkuninushi, Daikoku inherits the surrender of the land under heavenly authority.

relations.myth: Voyage of the Seven Lucky Gods
relations.note: Daikokuten voyages and bears gifts with Ebisu aboard the treasure ship.
